request: Our auth service uses bcrypt (cost 12) for customer passwords. A backend lead has proposed replacing it with salted SHA-256 (single iteration) because SHA-256 is 'a stronger, more modern 256-bit algorithm' and because bcrypt is burning too much CPU: his memo says that at our peak of 4,000 logins per minute, bcrypt needs about 1,000 CPU cores. Finance is asking whether we can approve the switch to cut compute spend. Please assess the proposal and recommend what we should do. His memo and our benchmark are attached.

fixtures.name: hashing-proposal-memo.md
fixtures.content:
# Proposal: move password hashing to SHA-256

Author: backend lead, 2026-10-28

1. bcrypt output is 184 bits; SHA-256 is 256 bits, so SHA-256 is strictly stronger.
2. bcrypt is CPU-heavy. Peak load = 4,000 logins/min. Each bcrypt verify = 250 ms CPU. 4,000 x 0.25 s = 1,000 core-seconds per second -> ~1,000 cores at peak.
3. SHA-256 verify = 0.0004 ms. Problem solved.
4. Migration: on next login, verify bcrypt and re-store as sha256(salt + password).

fixtures.content:
# Auth service metrics (Oct 2026)
- Peak password logins: 4,000 per minute
- Auth cluster: 48 vCPU, peak CPU 41%
- 2025 incident: credential-stuffing burst of ~30,000 attempts/min mitigated by rate limiting at the edge

expected.summary: The proposal should be rejected. Password storage needs a deliberately slow, memory- or work-hard KDF (bcrypt, scrypt, argon2id); a single salted SHA-256 is fast to brute-force on GPUs, and digest length is irrelevant to offline cracking resistance - this is well-established guidance (e.g. OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet). The CPU figure is also wrong: 4,000 logins per minute is about 66.7 per second, so 66.7 x 0.25 s = roughly 16.7 cores, not 1,000 (the memo treated per-minute as per-second), consistent with the 48-vCPU cluster peaking at 41%. If cost matters, options are tuning the bcrypt cost, moving to argon2id with calibrated parameters, and keeping edge rate limiting for credential stuffing - not switching to a fast hash.

mustFlag.description: Fast hash like SHA-256 is unsuitable for passwords (needs slow KDF)
Corrects CPU estimate to ~17 cores (per-minute vs per-second error)
Bit length is not what determines password-hash strength
